hook_text: Ten shillings a month, dawn to dusk in the cane, and jail if you left without a pass.
clip_script: Natal, the 1870s. A row of tin-roofed rooms beside the cane fields. Inside, families of indentured labourers who sailed from India. Before sunrise they walk out with cane knives. They work until dark, six days a week, and through the night when the mill is crushing. Miss a day sick and lose your pay. Leave without a pass and you can be jailed. But they push back: they complain to magistrates, they refuse to work, they build temples and keep their festivals alive. Their complaints reach India, which stops sending workers from 1866 until 1874. Then traders arrive who paid their own way, and settlers answer with a three-pound tax. A young lawyer called Gandhi joins the fight, and in 1914 the tax falls.
visual_style: A whiteboard row of barracks, a sun rising and setting over a cane field, a pass being stamped, then a temple drawn among the rooms and a tax notice being torn.
pacing: Slow and heavy for the daily routine, quickening through the resistance.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and hear how the workers pushed back.
